classes.name: Provincial and territorial general elections
classes.note: Counted per election, not per riding: each province's or territory's general election counts once, from the date list its elections agency or legislature publishes. An election counts once the archive holds its results. Yukon counts from 1909 and the Northwest Territories from 1975, when their councils became wholly elected. New Brunswick's agency lists its elections only from 1967, so its 24 earlier elections aren't counted yet. Where the official list gives only a month (Quebec in 1867 and 1871, Prince Edward Island in 1873), the election is dated to the first of that month.

classes.name: Provincial and territorial by-elections
classes.note: Each riding's by-election counts once. No national list of provincial by-elections exists; each agency lists its own, so this class has no enumerated dates yet.

classes.name: Federal referendums and plebiscites
classes.note: Three national votes: prohibition (1898), conscription (1942), and the Charlottetown Accord (1992, held outside Quebec, which voted the same day under its own law).

classes.name: Provincial and territorial referendums and plebiscites
classes.note: Called by each legislature under its own referendum act, so there is no regular cycle. Each question counts once. Quebec's 1980 and 1995 sovereignty referendums, British Columbia's electoral-reform votes (2005, 2009, and 2018), and Prince Edward Island's (2005, 2016, and 2019) are among those not yet held.

classes.name: Alberta Senate nominee elections
classes.note: Province-wide votes for nominees the Prime Minister is asked to appoint to the Senate, held alongside municipal (1989, 1998, and 2021) or provincial (2004 and 2012) elections.

dates.quote: October 16, 1989, in conjunction with the municipal elections
October 19, 1998, in conjunction with the municipal elections
November 22, 2004, in conjunction with the Provincial General Election
April 23, 2012, in conjunction with the Provincial General Election
October 18, 2021, in conjunction with the municipal elections

classes.name: Quebec municipal general elections (mayors and councils)
classes.note: Every local municipality under the Act respecting elections and referendums in municipalities elects its mayor and councillors on one fixed day; northern, Cree, and Naskapi villages vote under their own regimes. In 2025: 1,091 mayors and 6,795 councillors, with 41.3 percent turnout where the mayoralty was contested. By-elections count in the same class.

access.evidence: results by municipality for general and partial elections since November 2021, supplied by the municipalities

classes.finest_note: municipality and district from Élections Québec; Montréal by polling station

classes.name: Montréal borough mayors and borough councils
classes.note: Montréal's 19 boroughs elect their mayors and borough councillors on the municipal ballot.

access.evidence: votes by polling station for 2013, 2017, 2021, and 2025

classes.name: Quebec MRC prefects elected by universal suffrage
classes.note: A regional county municipality's prefect is either elected by universal suffrage or chosen by its council; 21 of the 87 MRCs elected theirs in 2025 (18 in 2021, 13 in 2009 to 2017, and 8 in 2005).

classes.name: Quebec French-language school board elections (commissioners)
classes.note: The French-language school boards elected commissioners on the first Sunday of November every four years; the last election held was 2 November 2014. The 2018 election was postponed to 1 November 2020 (SQ 2018, c. 15), and Loi 40 (SQ 2020, c. 1, sanctioned 8 February 2020) turned the boards into appointed school service centres and ended the 2020 election for them. The English-language boards kept elections (class qc_school).

cadence.locator: First Sunday of November every four years (2 November 2014); the 4 November 2018 election was postponed to 1 November 2020 by SQ 2018, c. 15, and cancelled for the French-language boards by SQ 2020, c. 1, so the row ends before 2018

classes.name: Quebec school board elections
classes.note: Since 2020 only the nine English-language school boards elect commissioners; French-language boards became appointed school service centres. The last elections were held on 2 November 2014 and 3 November 2024.

classes.name: Ontario municipal elections (heads of council and councils)
classes.note: All 444 municipalities elect on one regular voting day under the Municipal Elections Act, 1996, including the directly elected regional councillors and chairs of some upper-tier municipalities; terms were three years before 2006 and four since. By-elections count in the same class.

cadence.locator: Municipal Elections Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 32, Sched., as enacted (e-Laws version 1): s. 4 (1) a regular election is held in 1997 and in every third year thereafter; s. 5 voting day is the second Monday in November; s. 6 (1) a three-year term begins on December 1. Section 4 (1) was replaced by 2006, c. 9, Sched. H, s. 1 (2006 and every fourth year thereafter), so 2006 is the last triennial-cycle election

Municipal Elections Act, 1996, as consolidated from 1 January 2023 (e-Laws): s. 4 (1) a regular election is held in 2006 and in every fourth year thereafter (2006, c. 9, Sched. H, s. 1); s. 5 voting day is the fourth Monday in October (2009, c. 33, Sched. 21, s. 8 (4)), first applied in 2010

access.evidence: voters, turnout, and successful candidates by municipality; no candidate votes
poll-by-poll results for every candidate, 2003 to 2026

classes.finest_note: municipality from the province; Toronto by voting subdivision

classes.name: Ontario school board trustee elections
classes.note: Trustees of the 72 district school boards (31 English public, 29 English Catholic, 4 French public, and 8 French Catholic) are elected on the municipal voting day.

cadence.locator: Municipal Elections Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 32, Sched., as enacted (e-Laws version 1): s. 4 (1) a regular election is held in 1997 and in every third year thereafter; s. 5 voting day is the second Monday in November; s. 6 (1) a three-year term begins on December 1. Section 4 (1) was replaced by 2006, c. 9, Sched. H, s. 1 (2006 and every fourth year thereafter), so 2006 is the last triennial-cycle election

Municipal Elections Act, 1996, as consolidated from 1 January 2023 (e-Laws): s. 4 (1) a regular election is held in 2006 and in every fourth year thereafter (2006, c. 9, Sched. H, s. 1); s. 5 voting day is the fourth Monday in October (2009, c. 33, Sched. 21, s. 8 (4)), first applied in 2010

classes.name: British Columbia general local elections: mayors and councils
classes.note: The 161 municipalities elect mayors and councillors on general voting day; terms were three years until 2011 and four from 2014. Vancouver's elected Park Board and local community commissions vote on the same ballot.

classes.name: British Columbia regional district electoral area directors
classes.note: Each electoral area of the 27 regional districts elects one director on general voting day.

classes.name: British Columbia board of education trustee elections
classes.note: School trustees are elected on general voting day.

classes.name: Islands Trust trustee elections
classes.note: Local trust areas of the Islands Trust elect two trustees each on general voting day.

classes.name: Alberta municipal elections
classes.note: Cities, towns, villages, summer villages, specialized municipalities, and municipal districts (322 in all) elect councils under the Local Authorities Election Act, every four years since 2013. Summer villages vote in summer.
classes.finest_note: Calgary and Edmonton by voting station

classes.name: Alberta school board trustee elections
classes.note: Public and separate school board trustees are elected with the municipal councils under the Local Authorities Election Act.

classes.name: Alberta Metis Settlement council elections
classes.note: Each of the eight Metis Settlements elects its council under the Metis Settlements Act; the 40 councillors form the Metis Settlements General Council, whose officers are elected under its own policy.

classes.name: Saskatchewan urban and northern municipal elections
classes.note: Cities, towns, villages, and northern municipalities elect mayors and councillors every four years in November (2024-11-13, next 2028-11-08); resort villages vote in July. The 2015 Local Government Election Act governs.

classes.name: Saskatchewan rural municipality elections
classes.note: Rural municipalities elect councillors for half their divisions every two years (even divisions on 2026-11-09; reeves and odd divisions with the urban elections in 2028), each for a four-year term.

classes.name: Manitoba municipal elections
classes.note: Winnipeg and the 136 other municipalities elect mayors or reeves and councillors on one day; three resort communities vote in July.

classes.name: Manitoba school board trustee elections
classes.note: School trustees are elected with the municipal councils.

classes.name: New Brunswick local government and rural district elections
classes.note: Mayors, councillors, and rural district advisory committees are elected every four years; the reformed local governments first voted on 2022-11-28, and the general elections of 2021-05-10 and 2026-05-11 preceded and followed the reform. Elections New Brunswick runs and reports them.

cadence.locator: Municipalities Act, RSNB 1973, c. M-22, s. 38 (1) as replaced by SNB 2004, c. 2, s. 10: quadrennial elections on the second Monday in May for the year 2004 and every fourth year thereafter. The 2020 round (11 May) was postponed by An Act Respecting Elections in 2020, SNB 2020, c. 11, and held on 10 May 2021 (Elections New Brunswick report), so the row stops before 2020

access.evidence: event reports with poll-by-poll results and polling-division spreadsheets

classes.name: New Brunswick District Education Council elections
classes.note: District Education Council members are elected with the local governments.

classes.name: Nova Scotia municipal elections
classes.note: Mayors and councillors are elected every four years under the Municipal Elections Act; each municipality runs its own election and posts its results.

classes.name: Nova Scotia regional school board elections
classes.note: The seven English-language regional school boards were elected for four years on the municipal voting day (15 October 2016 was the last) and were replaced by regional centres for education on 1 April 2018 (Education Reform Act, Bill 72). The Conseil scolaire acadien provincial kept its elections (class ns_csap).

cadence.locator: Provincial release of 27 November 2015: the next municipal and school board elections take place on 15 October 2016; Bill 72 (2018) took effect on 1 April 2018 and replaced the school boards other than the CSAP. The row starts at 2016 because earlier cycles were not read

classes.name: Conseil scolaire acadien provincial member elections
classes.note: The francophone school board's members are elected on the municipal voting day.

classes.name: Prince Edward Island Legislative Council elections
classes.note: The upper house was elected, instead of appointed, from 1862 and merged with the House of Assembly in 1893 into the single Legislative Assembly, where each of the 15 districts elects one Assemblyman and one Councillor (those Councillor seats are part of the provincial general election, not this class). Candidates and voters needed property. No statute with a fixed election calendar has been read.

classes.name: Prince Edward Island municipal elections
classes.note: Every four years on the first Monday in November (2022-11-07 and 2026-11-02, next 2030-11-04). Elections PEI runs Charlottetown, Cornwall, Stratford, Summerside, and Three Rivers; the other municipalities run their own.

classes.name: Newfoundland and Labrador municipal elections
classes.note: Councils are elected every four years from 2001 on the last Tuesday in September; the 2025 election was deferred to 2 October, and local service districts voted for the first time.

classes.name: Yukon municipal elections
classes.note: Eight municipalities elect mayors and councils in October; terms moved from three to four years with the 2024 election (2021-10-21, 2024-10-17).

cadence.locator: Municipal Act, RSY 2002, c. 154, s. 52 before the 2023 amendment: a general election every third year on the third Thursday of October, starting in 2000 (read in the official consolidation; the file refuses scripted downloads, so the section number is unconfirmed)

classes.name: Northwest Territories community government elections
classes.note: Towns and villages elect councils for three-year terms in October (2024-10-21); hamlets vote in December with staggered terms, and charter communities and the Tłı̨chǫ communities set their own dates.

classes.name: Northwest Territories hamlet elections
classes.note: Hamlets vote on the second Monday in December under the Local Authorities Elections Act, while towns, villages, and cities vote on the third Monday in October (class nt_community). Terms are staggered and differ by office: in the round of 8 December 2025, mayors and half the councillors were elected for two years and the other half for three.

cadence.locator: Local Authorities Elections Act, RSNWT 1988, c. L-10, s. 10 (1) (b): the general election day for a hamlet is the second Monday in December (towns, villages, and cities vote on the third Monday in October, s. 10 (1) (a)). Hamlet terms are staggered and differ by office, so no period or phase is set; the 2025 round was held on 8 December 2025 (mayors and half the councillors for two years, the other half for three, Municipal and Community Affairs)

classes.name: Nunavut municipal elections
classes.note: The 25 municipal councils are elected every four years under the Nunavut Elections Act, run by Elections Nunavut (2023-10-23, next 2027-10-25).

classes.name: Municipal referendums and plebiscites
classes.note: Votes put to a municipality's electors (Quebec's approval referendums, Alberta and British Columbia plebiscites and assent votes, Ontario's municipal questions), held on general voting day or on their own.

classes.name: First Nations band council elections under the Indian Act and the First Nations Elections Act
classes.note: About 200 First Nations elect chiefs and councils every two years under the Indian Act, and those that opt in every four years under the First Nations Elections Act (2015). In 2015, 234 of 618 First Nations used the Indian Act and 2 the 2014 Act.
classes.disposition_reason: No central publisher: Indigenous Services Canada records who was elected but publishes no vote counts, and each First Nation posts its own results, often to members only.

classes.name: Self-governing and custom-code Indigenous government elections
classes.note: First Nations under custom election codes (344 in 2015) or self-government agreements (38), modern-treaty governments such as Nunatsiavut and Nisga'a Lisims, the Cree Nation Government, and the Métis Nation governments.
classes.disposition_reason: Each government runs its elections under its own constitution or code; no federal, provincial, or territorial agency runs or certifies them.
